title: Unfair Wealth, Patient Waiting, Shared Prayer
overview: James warns wealthy people who cheat their workers, then urges his readers to wait patiently for the Lord, speak honestly, and care for one another through prayer.

parts.label: Warning to the rich (vv. 1-6)
parts.note: James condemns wealthy landowners who hoarded goods until they rotted and held back their farm workers' pay, which the old law said must be paid before sunset. Most scholars think the condemned person who did nothing wrong stands for the innocent poor in general, while some Christians have read it as pointing to Jesus.

parts.label: Wait like a farmer (vv. 7-9)
parts.note: Farmers in Israel depended on autumn rains for planting and spring rains for ripening, so they had to wait for what they could not control. James asks his readers to wait that way for the Lord's return and not to turn their frustration on each other.

parts.label: Prophets and Job (vv. 10-11)
parts.note: The prophets were often mistreated for their message, and Job lost almost everything yet held on to God. James points to how Job's story ended as a sign that God is kind and merciful.

parts.label: Plain honest words (v. 12)
parts.note: People often swore by heaven or earth to make a promise sound more binding. Echoing Jesus, James says to be so honest that a simple yes or no is enough.

parts.label: Prayer, oil and healing (vv. 13-18)
parts.note: The sick could call the church's leaders, called elders, to pray and rub olive oil on them, and oil was a common medicine then. Scholars debate whether the oil here was meant as medicine, as a religious sign, or both, while Elijah's prayers about a drought show that an ordinary person's prayer matters.

parts.label: Bringing someone back (vv. 19-20)
parts.note: Helping someone who has drifted away to return is treated as saving them from ruin. Interpreters disagree whether the sins covered are those of the person brought back or of the one who helps.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether anointing the sick with oil is a lasting church practice with special spiritual power, as in the Catholic and Orthodox anointing of the sick, or a simple act of care tied to its time, and on how certain the promise of healing is.
think: When someone has been wronged and justice seems slow, what makes waiting bearable, and at what point does patience become something else?
